title: Inside Trump's American regime change
gist: A review of Haberman and Swan's 'Regime Change' arguing that the second Trump administration has concentrated war-and-peace decisions in the president and a handful of loyalists, politicised US intelligence to the point that CIA, State and Joint Chiefs warnings against the 2026 Iran strikes were simply overruled, and purged the ODNI and National Intelligence Council. The authors' core claim is that the presidency, not Trump, is what changed — and that the degraded intelligence feedback loop raises the odds of a strategic miscalculation with global consequences.

insights.claim: Politicising intelligence services creates an exponential feedback loop: analysts who are punished for inconvenient findings get worse at speaking truth to power, the president then receives worse information, makes worse decisions, and the cycle compounds.
insights.speaker: Matthew Hefler and John Sipher
insights.so_what: Degraded US intelligence quality raises the tail risk of a surprise geopolitical shock that markets have no early warning of; treat official US threat assessments as a less reliable signal than in prior administrations.
insights.quote: If one politicises the intelligence services by demanding they tell you what you want to hear, over time they become worse at speaking truth to power.
insights.locator: The president’s disregard of the nation’s intelligence services

insights.claim: Under the second Trump administration intelligence is valued for confirming the president's prior beliefs rather than for accuracy, with expertise and process treated as obstacles to be routed around.
insights.speaker: Matthew Hefler and John Sipher
insights.so_what: Expect US policy announcements to track the president's narrative needs rather than underlying facts — a reason to discount official framing of military or economic outcomes.
insights.quote: In that environment, intelligence is not valued because it is accurate. Rather, it is prized when it confirms what Trump believes.
insights.locator: In that environment, intelligence is not valued

insights.claim: Trump publicly pressured then-Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard to revise her assessment questioning whether Iran was close to a nuclear weapon, and the White House dismissed a leaked Defense Intelligence Agency report contradicting his claim that strikes had 'obliterated' Iran's nuclear capability as 'fake news'.
insights.speaker: Matthew Hefler and John Sipher
insights.so_what: Official claims about battle damage to Iranian nuclear infrastructure should be treated as contested; residual Iranian capability is an unpriced source of Middle East escalation risk.
insights.quote: The White House reacted furiously, calling the early ‘low confidence’ assessment ‘fake news’, threatening to subpoena reporters for their sources
insights.locator: Then a report from the Pentagon’s Defense Intelligence Agency

insights.claim: Trump's siding with Vladimir Putin over US intelligence at Helsinki in July 2018 is presented as the template for a pattern where the president rejects intelligence that threatens his own claim to legitimacy.
insights.speaker: Matthew Hefler and John Sipher
insights.so_what: Personal-legitimacy motives, not strategy, can drive US positioning toward Russia — relevant to handicapping any Ukraine or sanctions settlement.
insights.locator: Take his infamous decision in Helsinki in July 2018

insights.claim: In mid-February 2026 Netanyahu made a hard pitch for Trump to join an attack on Iran, and the next day Trump's own senior advisers dismantled the Israeli case — CIA Director John Ratcliffe called the regime-change proposal 'farcical' and Secretary of State Marco Rubio interjected that it was 'bullshit'.
insights.speaker: Matthew Hefler and John Sipher
insights.so_what: The most senior US national security principals opposed a war that happened anyway — internal dissent is no longer a brake, so escalation scenarios should be priced with a wider distribution.
insights.quote: CIA Director John Ratcliffe addressed Netanyahu’s optimistic proposal for regime change in Iran and called it ‘farcical’. To make the point, Secretary of State Marco Rubio interjected to say: ‘In other words, it’s bullshit.’
insights.locator: A critical moment came in mid-February 2026

insights.claim: Chairman of the Joint Chiefs General Dan Caine characterised Israeli overselling of military plans as standard operating procedure, saying the Israelis know they need US participation and therefore hard-sell it.
insights.speaker: Matthew Hefler and John Sipher
insights.so_what: A durable heuristic for reading Israeli operational claims — discount announced plan maturity when US backing is being sought.
insights.quote: in my experience, standard operating procedure for the Israelis. They oversell and their plans are not always well-developed. They know they need us and that’s why they’re hard selling
insights.locator: Others voiced similar scepticism

insights.claim: Trump launched the 2026 Iran war with no plan for the contingency in which regime change in Tehran failed to occur, and was indifferent to whether it happened at all.
insights.speaker: Matthew Hefler and John Sipher
insights.so_what: Open-ended conflicts without termination criteria tend to produce long-tailed energy and shipping risk; positioning for a clean resolution is unwarranted.
insights.quote: Nevertheless, Trump dismissed these warnings and launched the war anyway, unconcerned whether regime change in Tehran took place or not; there was no plan for war in the case that it did not.
insights.locator: Nevertheless, Trump dismissed these warnings

insights.claim: Senior US officials were unable to force serious planning around how Iran might block the Strait of Hormuz, despite raising concerns about the campaign.
insights.speaker: Matthew Hefler and John Sipher
insights.so_what: Hormuz closure risk was under-planned inside the US government — a direct read-through to oil, tanker rates and Gulf-exposed insurance.
insights.locator: The fact that senior officials such as Ratcliffe, Rubio and Caine

insights.claim: On Iran, key decisions were taken without disciplined intelligence process or strategic consensus, with senior officials excluded and neither Congress nor America's closest allies consulted.
insights.speaker: Matthew Hefler and John Sipher
insights.so_what: Allies discover US military action after the fact, which shortens the warning window for every other actor including markets.
insights.quote: Senior officials were excluded, and neither Congress nor America’s closest allies consulted.
insights.locator: On Iran, key decisions were reportedly not driven

insights.claim: Trump's response to Tucker Carlson's warning that the Iran war could ruin his presidency — 'Because it always is' — illustrates a decision style grounded in fatalistic confidence rather than analysis.
insights.speaker: Matthew Hefler and John Sipher
insights.so_what: A president who believes outcomes always break his way is more likely to take under-hedged risks; assume higher variance in US foreign policy.
insights.quote: Carlson asked how he knew. ‘Because it always is’, Trump replied.
insights.locator: When television personality Tucker Carlson phoned Trump

insights.claim: The central argument of 'Regime Change' is that Trump himself has not changed — the presidency has, because traditional norms, guardrails and mechanisms of accountability have been degraded.
insights.speaker: Matthew Hefler and John Sipher
insights.so_what: The institutional constraint premium that investors historically assumed for US policy has been removed and will not automatically return with a change of occupant.
insights.quote: Regime Change makes clear that it is not Trump that has changed but the presidency, since traditional norms, guardrails and mechanisms of accountability have been degraded.
insights.locator: Regime Change makes clear that it is not Trump

insights.claim: What distinguishes the second Trump term is scope rather than novelty: prior presidents have been domineering, clashed with Congress, or had adversarial relations with intelligence services, but none concentrated decision-making so fully in himself and a few loyalists.
insights.speaker: Matthew Hefler and John Sipher
insights.so_what: Historical-precedent arguments that 'this has happened before' understate the magnitude change — don't use past presidencies as base rates for policy volatility.
insights.quote: Many of the events and dynamics depicted here are not so much new phenomena in American history – rather, it is their scope.
insights.locator: Many of the events and dynamics depicted here

insights.claim: In Trump's first term, establishment figures actively obstructed him — Mark Milley saw his role as stopping the president from reckless action, and James Mattis promised to develop plans to assassinate Bashar al-Assad and then simply ignored the directive.
insights.speaker: Matthew Hefler and John Sipher
insights.so_what: The internal-sabotage buffer that once made extreme orders non-binding is gone; announced intentions now translate into action far more reliably.
insights.quote: argued vehemently with Trump and… saw his role as stopping the President from taking dangerous or reckless actions
insights.locator: These processes were in short enough supply in Trump 1.0

insights.claim: General Dan Caine offered only options rather than substantive advice before the 2026 Iran war and did not voice the full extent of his concerns, a deliberate contrast with Milley's interventionist model.
insights.speaker: Matthew Hefler and John Sipher
insights.so_what: Military leadership self-censorship means public signals of institutional dissent will be absent even when private opposition is strong.
insights.locator: Haberman and Swan highlight how this friction has been removed

insights.claim: Trump publicly misattributed to General Caine the view that the Iran war would be 'something easily won' — a claim Caine had never made — after Caine's private warnings leaked five days before the war.
insights.speaker: Matthew Hefler and John Sipher
insights.so_what: Attributed expert endorsement of US policy may be fabricated; verify the named official's own statements before treating them as confirmation.
insights.quote: The president simply rejected the reports and said that Caine believed the war would be ‘something easily won’ – something Caine had never actually said.
insights.locator: When the warnings he had voiced were published in the press

insights.claim: The National Security Council, which under previous administrations carried hundreds of staff drawn from across government, has become almost irrelevant under Trump 2.0, with conspiracy theorist Laura Loomer reportedly able to trigger NSC firings.
insights.speaker: Matthew Hefler and John Sipher
insights.so_what: The formal interagency channel no longer predicts policy; informal media-adjacent influencers are now a more accurate leading indicator of personnel and policy shifts.
insights.quote: ‘Why do we have the CIA when we have Laura Loomer?’
insights.locator: The National Security Council (NSC)

insights.claim: Trump reportedly nominated John Ratcliffe to lead the CIA on the condition that he would 'shred' the organisation, and used Tulsi Gabbard for 'personal-revenge missions'.
insights.speaker: Matthew Hefler and John Sipher
insights.so_what: Intelligence leadership appointments are being made for demolition and vendetta purposes, so agency output should not be read as an independent policy check.
insights.quote: Trump nominated John Ratcliffe to lead the CIA on the condition that he would ‘shred’ the organisation.
insights.locator: The same danger appears in Trump’s use of national security institutions

insights.claim: Tulsi Gabbard cut the 1,800-strong staff of the Office of the Director of National Intelligence by roughly 30 per cent before being fired.
insights.speaker: Matthew Hefler and John Sipher
entities: Office of the Director of National Intelligence
insights.so_what: A concrete measure of capacity destruction — roughly 540 analytic and coordination posts removed from the body that fuses US threat warning.
insights.locator: The president has appointed relatively inexperienced loyalists

insights.claim: Bill Pulte, former head of the Federal Housing Finance Agency, was appointed acting DNI with national security qualifications resting largely on pursuing the president's enemies, including criminal referrals of alleged mortgage fraud against Letitia James and Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook — neither of which has fared well in the courts.
insights.speaker: Matthew Hefler and John Sipher
insights.so_what: The same official who drove legal attacks on a sitting Fed governor now runs national intelligence — an explicit datapoint on the politicisation of institutions markets rely on for independence.
insights.locator: After firing Gabbard, Trump appointed former head

insights.claim: Twenty officials from the National Intelligence Council, including senior officers focused on Russia and China, were removed or chose to leave under the acting DNI's firings.
insights.speaker: Matthew Hefler and John Sipher
insights.so_what: The loss is concentrated in exactly the great-power accounts that drive tail risk — Russia and China analysis is now thinner precisely where it matters most.
insights.locator: One target has been the National Intelligence Council

insights.claim: Julia Curlee, a former director for intelligence programmes in the Trump White House, described the ODNI firings as performative rather than reform, arguing that sacking dozens of seasoned officers in a first week pleases a president who treats his own intelligence community as the enemy within.
insights.speaker: Matthew Hefler and John Sipher
insights.so_what: Criticism from inside the president's own former staff signals that the purge lacks even a nominal efficiency rationale defenders can rally around.
insights.quote: sacking dozens of seasoned officers in your first week isn’t reform – it’s performative firing to please a president who treats his own intelligence community as the enemy within
insights.locator: Speaking to the Washington Post, Julia Curlee

insights.claim: Even normally pliant Republican lawmakers balked at Pulte's appointment as acting Director of National Intelligence, yet the firings proceeded under Trump's instructions.
insights.speaker: Matthew Hefler and John Sipher
insights.so_what: Congressional discomfort is not translating into constraint — a marker of how little friction legislative objection now generates.
insights.locator: Despite the fact that normally pliant Republican lawmakers

insights.claim: Trump is characterised as 'programmable' rather than merely impulsive, making momentous decisions through a closed loop of grievance, flattery, conspiracy and personal loyalty, and responding to cues about who praises him or validates his suspicions rather than to facts.
insights.speaker: Matthew Hefler and John Sipher
insights.so_what: The highest-return lobbying channel is flattery and grievance-framing, not evidence — which is why access-driven actors can move US policy faster than institutions can.
insights.quote: He is unusually easy to manipulate because he responds less to facts than to cues – who praises him, who feeds his resentments, who validates his suspicions, who frames policy as revenge against his enemies.
insights.locator: While Trump can be impulsive

insights.claim: Trump displays a remarkable absence of ideology or belief system, with war-and-peace decisions often determined by whoever spoke to him last.
insights.speaker: Matthew Hefler and John Sipher
insights.so_what: Ideological models of US policy will misforecast; access and sequencing of meetings are better predictors than doctrine.
insights.quote: The book details how decisions over war and peace are often made depending on who last spoke to the president, who has no recognisable belief system nor ideology.
insights.locator: The consequences are not purely academic

insights.claim: Trump's legacy ambition operates on an earth-changing scale, extending to demands for the annexation of Greenland and Canada.
insights.speaker: Matthew Hefler and John Sipher
insights.so_what: Territorial demands on allies are a live policy input, not rhetoric — a persistent risk premium for Danish, Greenlandic and Canadian assets and for NATO cohesion.
insights.quote: a commitment to legacy on an earth-changing scale, demanding even the annexation of Greenland and Canada
insights.locator: What is new is the extent of the president’s personality quirks

insights.claim: Trump embraced a comparison of himself to Genghis Khan, Hitler and Alexander the Great as the most powerful man ever to live, attributing it to a 'historian' when it had actually been written by a former caddy of golfer Gary Player.
insights.speaker: Matthew Hefler and John Sipher
insights.so_what: Illustrates the low evidentiary bar for inputs that shape the president's self-image and therefore his policy choices.
insights.locator: Ghengis Khan. Adolf Hitler. Alexander the Great.

insights.claim: Many in the administration treat expertise as a sign of disloyalty and dissent as sabotage, leaving the White House vulnerable to manipulation by people with no business near serious national security decisions.
insights.speaker: Matthew Hefler and John Sipher
insights.so_what: Adversary influence operations have an unusually cheap entry point into US decision-making — a structural vulnerability that persists regardless of any single policy.
insights.quote: Many in the administration treat expertise as a sign of disloyalty and dissent as sabotage
insights.locator: The instinct of Trump and his small decision-making group

insights.claim: Haberman and Swan argue Trump was better off having lost the 2020 election to Biden, because it let him avoid Biden's troubles, regain control of the Republican Party after 6 January 2021, rehabilitate his failures through narratives like 'Stop the Steal', and assemble a team of diehard loyalists.
insights.speaker: Matthew Hefler and John Sipher
insights.so_what: Electoral defeat strengthened rather than ended a political project — a caution against assuming that losing an election removes a policy risk.
insights.quote: Trump was in fact fortunate to lose the 2020 election to Joe Biden, as this enabled him to position himself for his next run and construct a team of diehard supporters
insights.locator: Haberman and Swan make clear that, for all the irony

insights.claim: Congressional oversight has essentially collapsed under the current Republican majority in both chambers, and the authors' main hope for its return rests on an expected Democratic victory in the House at the 2026 mid-terms.
insights.speaker: Matthew Hefler and John Sipher
insights.so_what: The 2026 midterms are the single identified circuit-breaker for US executive discretion — a dated catalyst for policy-risk repricing.
insights.quote: which has essentially collapsed under the current Republican majority in both chambers of Congress
insights.locator: One must hope that Congressional oversight

insights.claim: The gravest and most enduring damage of Trump 2.0 may be to intelligence partnerships and institutional knowledge, since rebuilding relationships with agents and colleagues worldwide after rampant firings and a decline of international trust will take many years.
insights.speaker: Matthew Hefler and John Sipher
insights.so_what: Allied intelligence-sharing degradation is a multi-year structural change, not a cyclical one — relevant to European defence autonomy and intelligence-adjacent procurement.
insights.locator: But the harm inflicted on the intelligence and national security community

insights.claim: The rebuilding of the CIA's reputation after Vietnam, Nixon and the Church Committee is offered as the historical template for how recovery from the current damage might begin.
insights.speaker: Matthew Hefler and John Sipher
insights.so_what: Sets a realistic recovery horizon measured in decades, not electoral cycles.
insights.locator: The effort to rebuild the reputation of the CIA

insights.claim: Believing that historical contingency permanently favours you produces a hubris that is ultimately self-defeating — the authors' closing bet that the same luck that carried Trump will eventually turn against him.
insights.speaker: Matthew Hefler and John Sipher
insights.so_what: The article's implied view: current US policy dominance is luck-dependent and mean-reverting, so extrapolating the present configuration indefinitely is the error.
insights.quote: To imagine that a power as potent, complex and unpredictable as historical contingency is and will always remain on your side leads to a hubris that will, in the end, be self-defeating
insights.locator: Those in power today may think that history is always working out

insights.claim: The biggest downstream risk from the personalised presidency is that Trump blunders into strategic miscalculations that weaken American security and spark unpredictable global change.
insights.speaker: Matthew Hefler and John Sipher
insights.so_what: Frame US geopolitical risk as miscalculation risk rather than intent risk — hedges should target abrupt discontinuities, not gradual doctrine shifts.
insights.quote: Above all, he risks blundering into strategic miscalculations that could weaken American security and spark unpredictable global change.
insights.locator: From a national security perspective
